title: WPA Pre-Shared Key Cracked
description: wifite2 successfully recovered the WPA/WPA2/WPA3 pre-shared key (PSK) for the target SSID via offline dictionary attack against a captured 4-way handshake or PMKID. An attacker with this key can decrypt all past and future traffic on the network (unless PMF/forward secrecy is enforced) and authenticate as a legitimate client.
remediation: Replace the PSK with a strong random passphrase of at least 20 characters that does not appear in any common wordlist. Enforce WPA3-SAE where hardware supports it. Rotate the PSK immediately and audit which devices have stored it. Consider migrating to WPA3-Enterprise with certificate-based authentication for environments requiring stronger security.

title: WPA Handshake Captured
description: A complete WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake or PMKID was captured for the target SSID. While the PSK has not yet been recovered, the captured material can be subjected to unlimited offline brute-force or dictionary attacks without further access to the network. The handshake was obtained via deauthentication of a connected client or passive PMKID capture.
remediation: Change the WPA/WPA2 PSK to a strong, unique passphrase not present in public wordlists. Enable WPA3-SAE to replace the 4-way handshake authentication exchange with a forward-secret SAE commit/confirm protocol that is resistant to offline attacks. If WPA3 is not available, enforce a minimum passphrase length of 20+ characters drawn from a high-entropy random source.

title: WPA-Enterprise Credentials Captured
description: EAPHammer deployed a rogue AP that successfully impersonated the target WPA-Enterprise network, downgrades the 802.1X EAP exchange, and captured an MSCHAPv2 challenge/response or NTLM hash from an authenticating client. These hashes can be cracked offline or used directly in pass-the-hash attacks to authenticate to internal Windows/Active Directory resources.
remediation: Deploy client-side certificate validation to prevent clients from connecting to rogue APs: configure the supplicant to validate the RADIUS server certificate against a pinned CA certificate and reject connections when the certificate does not match. Disable weaker EAP methods (PEAP/MSCHAPv2, EAP-MD5) in favour of EAP-TLS with mutual certificate authentication. Train users not to dismiss certificate warnings.

title: WPA3 SAE Dragonblood — Invalid Curve Attack Confirmed
description: The target WPA3 SAE implementation accepted an invalid elliptic-curve point during the SAE Commit exchange (attack mode 1 — invalid curve). This is a variant of the Dragonblood vulnerability class disclosed by Mathy Vanhoef and Eyal Ronen. Exploitation allows an active attacker to trick the AP into performing computations on a weak curve, potentially leaking the password encoding and enabling offline dictionary attacks against WPA3 networks that were intended to be resistant to such attacks.
remediation: Apply firmware updates from the AP vendor that address CVE-2019-9494 and CVE-2019-9495. Ensure the WPA3 implementation validates that received curve points lie on the correct curve (point validation) before performing any SAE computations. Where firmware updates are unavailable, disable WPA3-SAE and use WPA2-Enterprise with EAP-TLS as a mitigation.

title: WPA3 SAE Dragonblood — Reflection Attack Confirmed
description: The target WPA3 SAE implementation is vulnerable to the SAE reflection attack (attack mode 0). By reflecting the AP's own SAE Commit message back to it, the attacking station tricks the AP into deriving the same PWE (Password Element), which can be used to authenticate without knowing the actual PSK under certain conditions. This is part of the Dragonblood vulnerability class (CVE-2019-9494).
remediation: Apply vendor firmware updates addressing CVE-2019-9494. The fix requires the AP to reject SAE Commit messages whose scalar and element fields match values it previously sent. Upgrade to a patched hostapd/wpa_supplicant version (2.10+).

title: WPA3 SAE Dragonblood — Secondary Invalid Curve Attack Confirmed
description: The target WPA3 SAE implementation is vulnerable to a secondary invalid curve attack variant (attack mode 2). This variant exploits the same class of point-validation weakness as CVE-2019-9495 but uses a different curve parameter manipulation technique, demonstrating that the AP's SAE implementation does not adequately validate curve points across multiple attack vectors.
remediation: Apply firmware updates that fully remediate CVE-2019-9495 across all SAE Commit handling code paths. Ensure the patched implementation performs explicit point validation on all received group elements before use in PWE derivation. Verify remediation by re-running dragonslayer attack modes 1 and 2.

title: WPA3 SAE Dragonblood — Zero-Scalar Attack Confirmed
description: The target WPA3 SAE implementation accepted a SAE Commit message with a zero scalar value (attack mode 3). Sending a scalar of zero forces the resulting shared key to be zero or a trivially predictable value, potentially allowing an attacker to authenticate without the actual PSK. This is a variant of the Dragonblood flaw class (CVE-2019-9500–9502).
remediation: Apply vendor firmware updates addressing CVE-2019-9500 through CVE-2019-9502. The AP must validate that received scalar values are within the valid range (1 ≤ scalar < order) and reject any Commit message with a scalar of zero or order.

title: WPA3 SAE Resource Exhaustion (Dragondrain) Tested
description: The target AP was subjected to the Dragondrain SAE commit-flooding attack (CVE-2019-9496). The AP was flooded with forged SAE Commit messages using spoofed source MAC addresses at high rate, targeting curve group 21 (521-bit elliptic). If the AP does not implement anti-clogging tokens or rate limiting, this causes CPU exhaustion and potential denial of service affecting legitimate clients.
remediation: Apply firmware updates that implement SAE anti-clogging (as specified in IEEE 802.11-2020 Section 12.4.6). Anti-clogging tokens force clients to echo a token before the AP performs expensive elliptic-curve computations, preventing CPU exhaustion. Also enable rate limiting on SAE Commit frames per source MAC address. Update to hostapd 2.10+ which includes anti-clogging support.

title: WPA2 KRACK Vulnerability — Standard 4-Way Handshake Reinstallation
description: The target client or AP is vulnerable to the KRACK key reinstallation attack targeting the standard 4-way handshake (CVE-2017-13077). By replaying and manipulating handshake message 3, an attacker can cause the client to reinstall an already-in-use pairwise transient key (PTK), resetting its associated nonce and replay counters. This allows the attacker to replay, decrypt, and potentially forge 802.11 frames.
remediation: Apply OS and driver security updates for all wireless clients that address CVE-2017-13077. On the AP side, apply firmware updates that prevent retransmission of handshake message 3 after the key has already been installed. For Android (especially 6.0), this vulnerability resulted in all-zero key reinstallation; priority patch Android devices. Verify remediation with the krackattacks test scripts.

title: WPA2 KRACK Vulnerability — TPTK Variant
description: The target is vulnerable to the KRACK Temporal PTK (TPTK) variant (CVE-2017-13078). This variant exploits the handling of message 1 of the 4-way handshake to cause nonce reuse in the PTK re-derivation process. The attacker can trigger a PTK reinstallation by injecting a retransmitted handshake message 1 with a replayed ANonce, forcing the client to reinstall an already-used key.
remediation: Apply security patches addressing CVE-2017-13078 for all affected wireless clients and APs. Ensure the supplicant implementation validates that new handshake sessions use fresh ANonces and that reinstallation of previously installed PTKs is prevented. Review and patch all wpa_supplicant and hostapd deployments to version 2.7+.

title: WPA2 KRACK Vulnerability — Group Key Reinstallation
description: The target is vulnerable to KRACK group key reinstallation (CVE-2017-13080). By replaying group key handshake message 1, an attacker can cause the client to reinstall an already-in-use group temporal key (GTK) with a reset replay counter. This allows the attacker to replay broadcast and multicast frames, which can be leveraged to inject ARP spoofing packets or perform other layer-2 attacks against all clients on the network.
remediation: Apply patches addressing CVE-2017-13080 for all wireless clients. The fix requires the supplicant to check whether the GTK being installed was already installed with the same key ID, and to reject reinstallation. Additionally, disable GTK rekeying on affected APs as a temporary mitigation until client patches are applied. Upgrade to wpa_supplicant 2.7+.

title: WEP Encryption in Use
description: The target network uses WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy), which has been cryptographically broken since 2001 (CVE-2001-0309). The RC4 stream cipher reuses 24-bit initialisation vectors (IVs), allowing the FMS, KoreK, and PTW statistical attacks to recover any WEP key from roughly 50 000 captured frames — achievable in under a minute on an active network. An attacker within radio range can decrypt all traffic and authenticate as a legitimate station. WEP was deprecated by IEEE 802.11i in 2004 and formally withdrawn. No patch exists; the protocol must be replaced.
remediation: Immediately replace WEP with WPA3-Personal (SAE) or at minimum WPA2-Personal (CCMP/AES). WEP cannot be patched — upgrade the AP firmware or replace the device. Segment any WEP-only legacy devices onto an isolated VLAN with no access to sensitive resources until they can be replaced.

title: WEP Key Cracked
description: aircrack-ng recovered the WEP key using the PTW statistical attack against collected IVs. With the key an attacker can decrypt all past and future traffic in real time, inject arbitrary 802.11 frames, and authenticate as a legitimate station. The network must be treated as fully compromised. All credentials, session tokens, and data transmitted over this network must be assumed captured by an adversary.
remediation: Treat the network as compromised. Replace WEP with WPA3-Personal immediately. Rotate all credentials used on devices that connected to this network. Review logs for unauthorised access since the network was deployed. Notify affected users. Replace hardware that cannot support WPA2.

title: Open / Unencrypted Wireless Network
description: The target network operates without wireless encryption (open authentication, no WEP/WPA). All data is transmitted in cleartext and can be captured passively by any device within radio range. HTTP sessions, credentials, emails, DNS queries, and file transfers are fully exposed without any evidence of interception.
remediation: Enable WPA3-Personal (SAE) or WPA2-Personal (CCMP/AES). If the network is intentionally open (guest portal, public hotspot), enforce TLS for all services, enable AP client isolation, and display a legal notice. Consider 802.11u Hotspot 2.0 / Passpoint for authenticated open networks that do not require a pre-shared key.

title: WPS Enabled on Access Point
description: Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is enabled on the target AP. WPS PIN-based authentication has a fundamental design flaw: the 8-digit PIN is verified in two independent 4-digit halves, reducing the effective keyspace from 10^8 to ~11 000 attempts. Many APs are additionally vulnerable to the Pixie-Dust attack (CVE-2014-9527), which recovers the WPS PIN offline in seconds from weak nonce values. A successful WPS attack recovers the full WPA2 PSK regardless of its length or complexity.
remediation: Disable WPS on the AP if it is not operationally required. If WPS is required, ensure the AP uses WPS 2.0 with lockout after 3 failed attempts and verify Pixie-Dust mitigation is implemented in the firmware. Apply all vendor firmware updates. Note: WPS cannot be safely enabled on APs with Broadcom or Ralink chipsets without explicit Pixie-Dust patches.

title: WPA3 Transition Mode — Downgrade Attack Surface
description: The target AP is operating in WPA3-Transition mode (WPA2/WPA3 mixed mode), simultaneously supporting both WPA2 and WPA3 clients. An attacker can deploy a rogue AP advertising only WPA2 with the same SSID. Clients configured for transition mode will connect via WPA2, exposing their 4-way handshake to standard offline dictionary cracking. This is the most practical WPA3 attack vector in real-world deployments. Tools: DragonShift, hostapd-mana.
remediation: Migrate to WPA3-only mode when all client devices support WPA3-SAE. In the interim, enable 802.11w (PMF) as mandatory — this prevents deauthentication-based downgrade forcing. Audit which clients cannot support WPA3 and establish a remediation timeline. Consider a separate SSID for legacy WPA2 clients rather than running mixed mode on the primary SSID.

title: WPA PMKID / EAPOL Hash Captured
description: hcxdumptool captured a PMKID or EAPOL hash for the target SSID without requiring a connected client or deauthentication. The PMKID is derived as HMAC-SHA1(PMK, 'PMK Name' || AP_MAC || CLIENT_MAC) and is broadcast by the AP in the first EAPOL frame. The captured hash can be subjected to unlimited offline brute-force or dictionary attacks against the WPA PSK without further access to the network.
remediation: Change the WPA PSK to a strong, randomly-generated passphrase of at least 20 characters not present in any wordlist. Enable WPA3-SAE to replace PMKID-based authentication with the Dragonfly PAKE, which is resistant to offline attacks. If WPA3 is unavailable, enforce a minimum passphrase entropy equivalent to >128 bits (20+ random characters from a large charset).

title: MSCHAPv2 Hash Cracked via asleap
description: asleap successfully cracked the MSCHAPv2 challenge/response captured by EAPHammer's rogue AP. MSCHAPv2 is inherently weak: the challenge is 56-bit DES-based and the response leaks the NT hash, which can be cracked offline in hours on consumer hardware. The recovered plaintext password can be used for pass-the-hash attacks against Windows/Active Directory resources, VPN authentication, and other services using the same credential.
remediation: Migrate from PEAP/MSCHAPv2 to EAP-TLS with mutual certificate authentication, which is not susceptible to rogue AP credential capture. If MSCHAPv2 must remain in use, configure clients to validate the RADIUS server certificate against a pinned CA and reject connections on certificate mismatch. Immediately rotate all affected credentials and audit for unauthorized access using the cracked password.

title: Rogue AP — Clients Associated to Evil Twin
description: One or more wireless clients associated to an attacker-controlled rogue AP that cloned the target SSID and BSSID. Clients that associate with the rogue AP have all their wireless traffic visible to the attacker; any unencrypted application-layer credentials or session tokens are exposed. Clients with stored network profiles are especially vulnerable as they connect automatically.
remediation: Deploy WPA3-SAE with PMF (802.11w) set to Required on all APs. Ensure clients validate network certificates where possible (WPA3-Enterprise or certificate-pinned supplicants). Implement wireless intrusion detection to alert on rogue APs. Educate users not to accept certificate warnings or dismiss security prompts on wireless networks.

title: Rogue AP — WPA Pre-Shared Key Phished via Captive Portal
description: A client associated with the rogue AP and submitted a WPA PSK via a captive portal page that mimicked the target network's authentication interface. The submitted credential was validated against the captured PMKID and confirmed as the correct pre-shared key. This attack requires no prior knowledge of the PSK and succeeds whenever a user can be deceived into re-entering their credentials after an unexpected disconnection.
remediation: Migrate to WPA3-SAE, which is not vulnerable to this class of credential phishing attack. As an interim control, restrict PSK distribution to trusted channels and train users to be suspicious of any captive portal requesting their Wi-Fi password. Enable WIDS/WIPS to detect and block rogue APs.

title: KARMA / MANA Attack — Client Credentials Captured
description: A KARMA/MANA rogue AP responded to probe requests from clients seeking previously associated networks and captured credentials from clients that automatically connected. This attack exploits devices that broadcast previously associated SSIDs in probe requests, allowing an attacker to impersonate any remembered network and intercept authentication material.
remediation: Configure client devices to send directed probe requests only (not broadcast) and to use random MAC addresses for probe requests. Disable auto-connect for open and low-trust networks. Enable PMF on all production networks. Ensure clients require server certificate validation before completing EAP authentication.

title: Protected Management Frames (PMF / 802.11w) Not Enforced
description: The target AP does not require Protected Management Frames (PMF/802.11w). A deauthentication or disassociation frame sent by an attacker was accepted by the AP or client, demonstrating that management frames are not authenticated. This allows an attacker in radio range to force client disconnections, enabling evil twin and MITM attacks.
remediation: Enable PMF (802.11w) set to Required on all enterprise APs. WPA3 mandates PMF by default. Verify that both AP and client supplicant support and enforce PMF. On WPA2 networks, set ieee80211w=2 in hostapd configuration.

title: BSS Transition Management (802.11v) Hijack Accepted
description: A crafted BSS Transition Management (BTM) request (802.11v, Category 10 Action 7) was accepted by a client, causing it to roam to an attacker-specified BSSID. This attack allows an attacker to redirect clients to a rogue AP without deauthentication, potentially bypassing PMF protections on WPA2 networks that do not protect Action frames.
remediation: Enable PMF Required (802.11w=2) to protect Action frames including BTM requests. Audit roaming policies and consider disabling 802.11v BTM on networks where roaming is not required. Upgrade affected clients and APs to firmware versions that validate BTM request authenticity.

title: Client Probe Request Harvest — Remembered Network Disclosure
description: Wireless clients in the vicinity are broadcasting probe requests containing the SSIDs of previously associated networks. This information discloses the wireless networks a device has connected to, can be used for device tracking (even with MAC randomisation if implementation is flawed), and enables targeted KARMA/evil twin attacks against those specific SSIDs.
remediation: Configure devices to send only directed probe requests to specific APs rather than broadcast probes for all remembered networks. Modern operating systems with MAC randomisation also suppress SSID disclosure in probes — ensure this feature is enabled. Remove outdated or low-trust networks from device preferred network lists.

title: EAP Downgrade — Weak EAP Method Credentials Captured
description: EAPHammer with balanced negotiation captured credentials by accepting a weaker EAP method (e.g. PEAP/MSCHAPv2 or EAP-MD5) offered by a client whose supplicant was not locked to a specific EAP type. MSCHAPv2 hashes obtained this way can be cracked offline or relayed directly to Windows domain services without cracking.
remediation: Lock client supplicants to a specific permitted EAP method and enforce server certificate validation. Disable weaker EAP types (PEAP/MSCHAPv2, EAP-FAST without PAC validation, EAP-MD5) at both the RADIUS server and client policy levels. Migrate to EAP-TLS with mutual certificate authentication where possible.

title: SAE Transition Mode — WPA2 Downgrade Attack Surface
description: The target AP operates in WPA3/WPA2 transition mode and a WPA2-only rogue AP was created with the same SSID. Clients supporting both WPA3-SAE and WPA2-PSK may associate with the rogue WPA2-only AP, losing the security guarantees of SAE. This enables legacy WPA2 attacks including PMKID capture and handshake-based cracking against previously WPA3-protected clients.
remediation: Disable WPA3/WPA2 transition mode and enforce WPA3-SAE only once all clients support it. If transition mode is required, enable PMF Required (802.11w=2) on both the WPA2 and WPA3 BSSIDs. Implement WIDS to detect duplicate SSIDs advertising different security capabilities.

title: ARP Cache Poisoning — MITM Position Established
description: ARP cache poisoning was successfully performed on the rogue AP's subnet, placing the assessment system in a man-in-the-middle position between wireless clients and the gateway. All unencrypted traffic (HTTP, FTP, Telnet, legacy protocols) was readable, and encrypted traffic was subject to downgrade or stripping attacks. This demonstrates the risk of any attack scenario where a client can be induced to join an attacker-controlled network.
remediation: Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches. Deploy HTTPS Strict Transport Security (HSTS) and HSTS preloading to prevent protocol downgrade. Ensure all internal services use TLS. On wireless networks, WPA3-SAE with PMF prevents the initial rogue AP association that enables this attack.

title: LLMNR / NBT-NS Poisoning — NTLMv2 Hashes Captured
description: Responder successfully poisoned LLMNR (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution) and/or NBT-NS (NetBIOS Name Service) queries on the rogue AP's subnet and captured NTLMv2 challenge/response hashes from Windows clients attempting to resolve non-existent hostnames. These hashes can be cracked offline or used in NTLM relay attacks to authenticate to internal services without cracking.
remediation: Disable LLMNR via Group Policy: Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Network → DNS Client → Turn Off Multicast Name Resolution = Enabled. Disable NBT-NS via WINS settings on the IPv4 adapter: disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP. Implement SMB signing to prevent NTLM relay attacks. Monitor for and alert on unexpected LLMNR/NBT-NS query responses.

title: Internal Hosts Discovered via Post-Connection Port Scan
description: An nmap scan of the wireless subnet revealed live hosts and open services accessible to wireless clients. This establishes the attack surface available to any client (authorised or rogue) that connects to the wireless network. Services accessible from the wireless segment without additional segmentation represent a potential lateral movement path.
remediation: Implement network segmentation: place the wireless network in a dedicated VLAN with firewall rules restricting access to internal services. Apply the principle of least privilege — wireless clients should only be able to reach services required for their function. Disable unnecessary services on hosts and implement host-based firewalls.

title: TKIP Encryption in Use
description: The target network uses TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol), a deprecated encryption scheme that was introduced as a quick fix for WEP and was officially deprecated by the IEEE 802.11 standard in 2012. TKIP is vulnerable to the Beck-Tews and Ohigashi-Morii attacks (ChopChop/fragmentation), allowing an attacker to partially decrypt and inject short packets without the key.
remediation: Disable TKIP and require CCMP (AES) as the only permitted pairwise cipher. Set rsn_pairwise=CCMP and wpa_pairwise=CCMP in hostapd configuration, or equivalent settings in the AP's admin interface. Remove WPA1/TKIP-only client support — all modern clients support CCMP.

title: TKIP ChopChop / Fragmentation Attack — Packet Decryption Confirmed
description: A TKIP ChopChop or fragmentation attack (Beck-Tews / Ohigashi-Morii) was confirmed against the target network. An attacker can exploit this to decrypt the last 12 bytes of an arbitrary short packet without knowing the key, and to inject up to 7 or 14 bytes of attacker-chosen plaintext per minute. This enables ARP poisoning, DNS spoofing, and decryption of short high-value packets (e.g. ARP replies, DNS responses) on WPA-TKIP networks.
remediation: Immediately disable TKIP. Migrate the network to WPA2 or WPA3 using only CCMP (AES) as the pairwise cipher. Do not allow TKIP as a fallback cipher for any client.

title: Wi-Fi Direct / P2P Device Discovered
description: A Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) capable device was discovered in the assessment area. Wi-Fi Direct devices create their own access point interfaces and may accept WPS-PIN connections independently of the corporate wireless infrastructure, bypassing network access controls and firewall policies. If WPS-PIN is enabled, the device may be vulnerable to the Pixie Dust or online WPS brute-force attacks.
remediation: Disable Wi-Fi Direct on corporate devices via MDM or Group Policy where the feature is not required. If Wi-Fi Direct is necessary, ensure WPS-PIN is disabled and only WPS-PBC (push button) is permitted. Audit firmware for Wi-Fi Direct devices and apply vendor security updates.

title: Wi-Fi Direct WPS PIN Cracked — Device Compromised
description: The WPS PIN for a Wi-Fi Direct device was recovered via reaver or a Pixie Dust offline attack. An attacker with this PIN can authenticate to the device's P2P group owner and gain network-level access to the device, potentially enabling access to shared files, printers, or other services exposed over the P2P connection.
remediation: Disable WPS on all Wi-Fi Direct capable devices. If WPS must remain enabled for operational reasons, disable PIN mode and use only WPS-PBC (push button) with physical access controls. Apply vendor firmware updates to devices vulnerable to Pixie Dust.

title: Captive Portal Bypass Confirmed
description: The target captive portal was bypassed using one or more techniques: DNS tunnelling (exfiltrating data via DNS queries to an external resolver), MAC address spoofing (cloning the MAC of an already-authenticated client), or direct HTTPS access to allowed domains before portal authentication. This allows an attacker to gain full internet access without completing the required authentication or payment flow.
remediation: Enforce captive portal controls at the IP layer rather than relying solely on DNS. Block all outbound DNS except to the captive portal resolver. Implement MAC address validation in conjunction with IP binding and session tokens. Use HTTPS for the captive portal itself to prevent credential interception.
